newsitem.title: UK: UK Labour warns of "loony" Conservative right.
newsitem.headline: UK Labour warns of "loony" Conservative right.

text.p: Britain's main opposition Labour party sought on Friday to bolster its commanding poll lead by warning that the ruling Conservatives would swing sharply to the right if they retained power at the coming election.

In its latest pre-election salvo, Labour said new government plans to privatise parts of the welfare state showed the Conservative party was now in thrall to right-wing dogmatists who would have been dismissed as "loony" five years ago.
"Who can imagine how much further to the right the Tory party will swing over the next five years if they get back in again?" Labour's foreign affairs spokesman, Robin Cook, said.

Cook was speaking at a news conference timed to coincide with the start of the Conservatives' Central Council meeting in Bath, at which the ruling party's leaders are expected to stress that while they offer stability, Labour posed only risks.

But Cook said: "The truth is the Tory party cannot now pretend that a vote for the Conservatives is a vote for the status quo. A vote for the Conservatives is a vote for increasingly loopy ideas from the far right and for further disruption of public services."
Cook speculated that, even if re-elected, Prime Minister John Major would not survive the shift to the right and would step down before the end of the five-year parliamentary term.
"A vote for John Major risks being a vote for Michael Portillo as prime minister," Cook said.
Right-wing Defence Secretary Michael Portillo, an erstwhile protege of ex-prime minister Margareth Thatcher, is expected to contest the Conservative leadership if and when Major quits.
Labour, in opposition since 1979, leads the Conservatives by about 25 percentage points according to recent surveys, including a Harris poll in Friday's Independent newspaper.

But Labour leader Tony Blair has repeatedly warned his troops against complacency and exhorted them both to spell out Labour's policies and keep up the pressure on their opponents in the run-up to the election, widely expected to be on May 1.
Labour's economics spokesman, Gordon Brown, said Britain would be taking a leap in the dark if it gave the Conservatives an unprecedented fifth straight term of office.

"If the British people were ever to return John Major to Downing Street with a licence to privatise the basic state pension, old people's homes and home-helps, Britain will move from the current age of insecurity under the Tories to an age of fear," Brown told the same news conference.
